clue.text: Frenchman walked back outside to disappear

indicators.note: outside means the turned word is wrapped around the Frenchman's letter
back tells us the word for walked is read from its end to its start

parts.note: walked up and down is paced
M is the abbreviation of Monsieur, a Frenchman's title

explanation.surface: A Frenchman retraces his steps and then vanishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns PACED into DECAP, and 'outside' puts it round M.
explanation.definitionFit: To decamp is to leave suddenly or secretly, to vanish from a place.

clue.text: Level the score in match

parts.note: a plain description of drawing level with the opposing team during a game

explanation.definitionFit: To bring the scores level in a game, typically by scoring a goal.

clue.text: Is "charm" a new version of an old word?

indicators.note: a new version of the words is a reworking of their letters into fresh order

explanation.surface: A question of whether the word charm is an antiquated term.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaism is an obsolete expression kept for effect in modern speech.

clue.text: Forerunner — before (or after) the dogs

indicators.note: after places the word or behind the dogs in the answer

parts.note: pre is the Latin prefix for before
curs are mongrel dogs

explanation.surface: A runner that comes before or after the greyhounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(or after)' reads as an aside allowing either order, but 'or' is a piece and 'after' says where it goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A precursor is one who goes ahead, heralding a later arrival.

clue.text: Bird authority, extremely ethical

parts.note: Edward Cocker wrote a famous arithmetic book; 'according to Cocker' is an old British phrase meaning correct by the rules

indicators.note: extremely means take the letters at the extremes, first and last, of ethical

explanation.surface: An ornithological expert is said to be scrupulously moral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'according to Cocker' (Edward Cocker, a 17th-century author of an arithmetic book) is an old British phrase for 'correct', so Cocker stands for an authority. 'extremely' takes the first and last letters of 'ethical', EL.
explanation.definitionFit: A young male domestic fowl, a kind of farmyard bird.

clue.text: Walton's way to fish?

parts.note: Izaak Walton subtitled his angling classic The Compleat Angler 'the Contemplative Man's Recreation', so his way of fishing was thoughtful

explanation.definitionFit: Izaak Walton's 17th-century book on angling calls fishing the recreation of a thoughtful, reflective man.

clue.text: Nuclei of officers, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word for officers is heard rather than read

parts.note: colonels are senior army officers

explanation.surface: The core of the officer corps, so to speak.
explanation.definitionFit: Kernels are central cores, as of a seed or of an argument.

clue.text: Sort to resist a poet and painter

indicators.note: sort means put in order, so the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: A command to arrange things in order to fight off an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a Victorian Pre-Raphaelite who both wrote verse and painted.

clue.text: Purify-of desire to scold

parts.note: lust is strong desire
to rate someone is to scold them angrily, an old usage

explanation.surface: A plea to cleanse oneself of the urge to nag.
explanation.definitionFit: To lustrate is to purify by a ritual offering or washing.

clue.text: Drink time — big cask wanted

parts.note: punch is a mixed drink served from a bowl
an eon is a vast stretch of time

explanation.surface: A thirsty call for a drink and a large barrel to hold it.
explanation.definitionFit: A puncheon is a large barrel for liquids such as rum or wine.

clue.text: Turning-point about a certain river

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
R is the abbreviation for river
the Isis is a particular river, the Thames as it passes Oxford

explanation.surface: A decisive moment arrives near some particular river.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: R for river, and ISIS as the certain river, the name the Thames takes at Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is the decisive moment when events turn for better or worse.

clue.text: An excuse, of course, for diversion

parts.note: a plea is an excuse offered in defence
sure, as a reply, means of course

explanation.surface: Someone offers a pretext for some amusement, naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: A diversion is an amusement or entertainment, a source of enjoyment.

clue.text: Man in last place to try once more

indicators.note: in means the word for man sits inside the word for last place

parts.note: the rear is the last position in a line
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A competitor finishing last wants another go.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehear a case is to try it again in court, hearing it a second time.

clue.text: His rolling stone gathered no moss

definitions.text: His rolling stone gathered no moss

parts.words: His rolling stone gathered no moss
parts.note: the proverb is turned on the Greek king condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever: his stone never stopped long enough to gather moss

explanation.surface: A twist on the proverb about the rolling stone.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth this king was punished in Hades by pushing a boulder up a hill, only for it to roll back each time.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure of myth whose eternal punishment was rolling a stone uphill.

clue.text: A remarkable person climbs on it somehow, howling

indicators.note: in a down clue climbs means the letters go upwards, read in reverse

parts.note: a lulu is an outstanding person or thing

indicators.note: somehow says the words on it are put into some other order

explanation.surface: An impressive figure clambers aboard and wails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbs' turns ALULU into ULULA; 'somehow' turns ONIT into TION.
explanation.definitionFit: Ululation is a wailing or loud lamenting cry.

clue.text: Tiller in old tin hat

definitions.meaning: the steering gear of a boat, of which the tiller is the handle
an archaic word for a helmet, a metal headpiece

explanation.definitionFit: A tiller is the lever that steers a boat, and a helmet, the soldier's tin hat, was once called by this shorter word.

clue.text: Hooter broadcast from a tree

parts.note: a horn is a hooter, as on a car
to beam a programme is to transmit it

explanation.surface: A car horn sounding out from a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The hornbeam is a hardwood tree of the birch family.

clue.text: Persistent wish to wash up

parts.note: to long is to wish for

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for wash is read from the bottom

parts.note: lave is a literary word for wash

explanation.surface: Someone keeps on wanting to do the dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Longeval means long-lived, so lasting or enduring.

clue.text: Depravity is very sweet

parts.note: an ice is a frozen sweet, a dessert

explanation.surface: Wickedness is described as extremely sugary.
explanation.definitionFit: Vice is immoral or wicked behaviour, moral corruption.

clue.text: Competed, ardour rising within, and made good

indicators.note: within means the turned word sits inside the word for competed

parts.note: vied means competed

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: fire is passion or ardour

explanation.surface: A contestant, passion growing inside, succeeded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' reverses the passion word upwards in this down clue, and 'within' tucks the result inside the word for competed; 'made good' means proved, not repaired.
explanation.definitionFit: To verify is to confirm or substantiate, so verified means borne out or proved true.

clue.text: Nostrums the secular Left push out

indicators.note: push out suggests forcing the letters out of their order into a new one

explanation.surface: A political note on how the secular left rejects quack remedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Nostrums are patent medicines or panaceas claimed to fix everything.

clue.text: Make a fuss about football back — a low fellow

indicators.note: about means the word for making a fuss goes around the other letters

parts.note: to create is to make a fuss or complain noisily

indicators.note: back tells us the football letters are read in reverse

parts.note: RU is short for Rugby Union, a code of football

explanation.surface: A footballer's complaint about a defender, said to be a lowlife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'football' is the rugby code here, and 'back' reverses its letters before 'about' wraps the fuss word round them.
explanation.definitionFit: Creature is used contemptuously for a despised or servile person.

clue.text: Used by Peeping Tom on the highway?

definitions.text: Used by Peeping Tom on the highway?

parts.words: Used by Peeping Tom on the highway?
parts.note: a tom is a male cat, so a peeping tom cat looks with its eye; on the road, reflective studs bear that name

explanation.definitionFit: Reflective road studs are named after a feline's eye that glows in headlights.

clue.text: Calendar the West is out to nullify

indicators.note: is out means the letter for the West is dropped from the name

parts.note: the Newgate Calendar was a famous record of crimes from London's Newgate prison
W is the abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: Someone sets about wiping out a western diary.
explanation.walkthrough: The Newgate Calendar, an 18th- and 19th-century London bestseller of criminals' lives, lets 'Calendar' stand for NEWGATE; 'is out' drops its W.
explanation.definitionFit: To negate something is to cancel its effect, making it void.

clue.text: Gin made one cock-eyed, it's thought

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: cock-eyed means askew, so the letters are set crooked into a new order

explanation.surface: A drink of gin has someone fancying things.
explanation.definitionFit: Imagined means supposed or conceived in the mind, so believed rather than seen.

clue.text: Grudgingly admired. I've changed in consequence

indicators.note: in means the reworked letters go inside the word for consequence

parts.note: an end is an outcome or result

indicators.note: changed signals that the letters of I've are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone admits a change of attitude as a result of resentment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges I'VE (the apostrophe is ignored), and 'in' places the result inside the word for consequence.
explanation.definitionFit: To envy someone is to resent their good fortune while coveting it.

clue.text: Qualified to be a partner, this worthy

definitions.meaning: suitable to be chosen as a husband or wife, as in a desirable bachelor
fit or deserving to be chosen

explanation.definitionFit: An eligible bachelor is a desirable match, and an eligible candidate is fit and deserving of selection.

clue.text: Fruit used for port made during war

definitions.meaning: a dark berry from a tree of the genus Morus
the prefabricated harbours towed to Normandy in 1944 were codenamed after this tree

explanation.definitionFit: The berry grows on a tree whose name was given to the floating harbours used after D-Day in the Second World War.

clue.text: Having swellings, being without medicine?

parts.note: no means without any, as in no money
a dose is a measured quantity of medicine

explanation.surface: Someone with lumps who has had no treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Nodose, from the Latin for knot, describes something knotty or knobbed with lumps.
